title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
headline: A language model's error drops along a clean, predictable line as you grow its size, its data, or its compute, and the best way to spend a fixed compute budget is to mostly build a bigger model.
abstract: We study empirical scaling laws for language model performance on the cross-entropy loss. The loss scales as a power-law with model size, dataset size, and the amount of compute used for training, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. Other architectural details such as network width or depth have minimal effects within a wide range. Simple equations govern the dependence of overfitting on model/dataset size and the dependence of training speed on model size. These relationships allow us to determine the optimal allocation of a fixed compute budget. Larger models are significantly more sample-efficient, such that optimally compute-efficient training involves training very large models on a relatively modest amount of data and stopping significantly before convergence.

images.alt: A row of clay-orange dots descends in a dead-straight line down a pixel mountain slope from upper-left to lower-right, with inked loss and scale axes, showing that a model's error falls along a clean straight power law as you grow its scale.
images.caption: Grow the scale and the loss falls along a straight line, the same line over six orders of magnitude.

images.alt: A pixel sack of flour labelled compute splits with a thick clay-orange arrow into a large layer cake labelled model and a thin sage arrow into a tiny scoop of batter labelled data, showing that a fixed compute budget is best spent mostly on a bigger model and only a little on more data.
images.caption: A fixed compute budget splits best when most of it builds a bigger model and only a little buys more data.

images.alt: A large clay-orange pixel sponge towers over a tiny sage-green puddle, with an ink brace and arrow marking the gap, showing that a model far too big for its dataset runs out of data to learn from and starts to overfit.
images.caption: A model far bigger than its dataset runs dry and starts to memorize, which the L(N, D) law predicts exactly.
